crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Self-Driving Laboratories
children.blurb: Self-driving laboratories are lab systems where software plans experiments, robots execute them, and instruments measure results without a human moving every sample.

children.name: Digital Twins for Experiments
children.blurb: Digital twins for experiments are computational models of a physical experiment, instrument, or sample that stay synchronized with real data.

children.name: Instrument and Sensor Data
children.blurb: Instrument and sensor data is the stream of measurements that laboratory instruments and sensors produce, together with the context that makes those measurements meaningful.

children.name: Optimising Lab Protocols
children.blurb: Optimising lab protocols covers the design, scheduling, and revision of experimental procedures so that they use less time, reagent, and labour while producing more reliable results.

children.name: Forecasting Lab Supplies
children.blurb: Forecasting lab supplies covers the prediction of demand for reagents, consumables, and small equipment in a laboratory, from pipette tips and culture plates to antibodies and solvents.

sections.body: Laboratory automation and simulation is the part of AI research that connects physical lab work with computational models. In practice, AI systems now schedule robotic liquid handlers, choose which experiments to run next, and adjust protocols when results drift. Self-driving laboratories combine robots, sensors, and machine learning so that a closed loop can propose, run, and analyse experiments with limited human input. Digital twins for experiments build software replicas of instruments or processes, then use those replicas to test conditions before they are tried on real samples. Instrument and sensor data work turns raw readings from spectrometers, microscopes, and environmental monitors into clean inputs for models. Forecasting lab supplies uses demand patterns and lead times to predict when reagents, plates, or consumables will run short.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The field has real momentum, but it is not a solved problem. Closed-loop labs work best for well-defined tasks such as crystallisation screens or simple chemical reactions, where the search space is bounded and the readout is fast. Many systems still depend on human technicians to prepare samples, fix errors, and maintain instruments, so full autonomy is rare. Digital twins are useful when the underlying physics is understood, yet they struggle with messy biological systems, unexpected contamination, or equipment that changes over time. Instrument data pipelines often break when formats differ between vendors or when calibration drifts, and protocol optimisation can overfit to a narrow set of conditions. Supply forecasting is limited by unreliable delivery data and by sudden shortages that no historical pattern can predict. The honest limit is that these tools assist and accelerate laboratory work, they do not replace scientific judgement.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages in this section fit together as a chain from physical execution to planning. Self-Driving Laboratories is the entry point for readers who want to understand how robots and AI close the experiment loop. Digital Twins for Experiments explains how virtual copies are built and where they can substitute for costly physical trials. Instrument and Sensor Data covers the messy middle, the capture, cleaning, and calibration of readings that every other page depends on. Optimising Lab Protocols shows how AI searches for better sequences, temperatures, and timings once reliable data is available. Forecasting Lab Supplies looks outward to the logistics that keep a lab running, using the same predictive methods on inventory and delivery records. A reader can start with any page, but the section is strongest when read as a connected workflow, and the library's 135 research papers provide the underlying evidence for the claims made across these topics.
